items.title: What happened in F1 Mexican GP final practice
items.author: Jack Cozens
items.content:
Lando Norris and Kimi Antonelli were near-inseparable in final practice for Formula 1's Mexican Grand Prix as Ferrari's pace faltered ahead of qualifying.

Friday pacesetter Charles Leclerc ultimately ended up third for Ferrari, but only at the end of the session following aborted attempts at his qualifying simulation on soft tyres.

He and team-mate Lewis Hamilton - whose session played out in a similar way - had traded fastest times at the beginning of FP3 as the top teams all chose to start the session on medium tyres.

Mercedes was among the first of the frontrunners to switch to softs and while George Russell pondered whether a double-prep lap was necessary, telling the team to consider telling Antonelli to push after a single warm-up lap, Antonelli did complete two prep laps and duly went fastest with a 1m17.601s.

That looked as though it would stand as the session's best time until Norris improved with two minutes left of the hour-long session, going one thousandth quicker for McLaren.

Leclerc was 0.117s back in third, suggesting the Ferrari will remain a contender for pole in qualifying, while Oscar Piastri ended the session within two tenths of his pacesetting McLaren team-mate in fourth.

Max Verstappen complained of brake issues late on and was three and a half tenths down in fifth ahead of Hamilton, with less than seven hundredths covering the Ferrari in sixth and Arvid Lindblad at the back of the top 10, as Racing Bulls again had both drivers inside the theoretical Q3 cutoff.

Lindblad and ninth-fastest Lawson were well clear of their midfield rivals, with Nico Hulkenberg four tenths further back for Audi ahead of Alpine duo Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly and Fernando Alonso's Aston Martin.

Hulkenberg set the joint-highest number of laps in the session (32) alongside Ryo Hirakawa, parachuted in to the second Haas seat for the remainder of the weekend with Esteban Ocon replaced ahead of FP3.

Hirakawa ran through a full programme including plenty of opportunities for single push laps, and by the end of a session where he used three sets of softs had a best time of 1m19.504s that left him 19th, 1.904s off the pace and inside six tenths of team-mate Ollie Bearman.

Home driver Sergio Perez was one of two drivers, alongside Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto, who failed to set a time.

Perez completed just one installation lap before returning to the Cadillac garage, where the team opted to make a precautionary engine change before qualifying.

His team-mate Valtteri Bottas was 20th, 2.742s off the pace and 0.838s behind Hirakawa.

items.title: Hadjar escapes with warning for pushing Mexico F1 paddock guest
items.author: Jack Cozens
items.content:
Isack Hadjar has been given a formal warning for pushing a guest in the paddock ahead of the first Formula 1 practice session at the Mexican Grand Prix.

Footage circulated on social media on Friday that appeared to show Hadjar pushing someone who had tried to take a selfie with him.

The Red Bull driver was subsequently called to see the F1 stewards on Saturday morning for what the summons document described as 'alleged misconduct'.

Hadjar stated in his appearance in front of the stewards that he was running late for FP1 and, having stopped for a photograph with a young fan, was "approached by a paddock guest in an aggressive manner".

The stewards' document detailing that account also said "one security person was walking behind him [Hadjar] and was unable tointervene and prevent what was tantamount to an invasion of the driver's private space".

Having initially resisted that move, Hadjar subsequently "pushed him aside with his open right hand" - a breach of article 12.2.1.l of the FIA international sporting code relating to misconduct.

However, in awarding only a warning the stewards acknowledge five mitigating circumstances in Hadjar's favour, in line with the guidelines in appendix B of the ISC.

These were that Hadjar was "reacting to an uninvited and rather aggressive action by another person"; that he was trying to make his way to the Red Bull garage for FP1 through a congested area; that he did not have "sufficient" security present; that the guest invaded his personal space without consent; and the "general issue" drivers have moving through the paddock.

items.title: All the reasons the Ocon-Haas relationship fell apart
items.author: Ben Anderson
items.content:
Haas is staying tight-lipped, but its sudden decision to replace Esteban Ocon with Ryo Hirakawa at Formula 1's Mexican Grand Prix suggests its regular (and soon-to-be-former) driver has been benched.

In this piece, first published at the end of September when Ocon's end-of-2026 exit was announced, Ben Anderson and Scott Mitchell-Malm look at how the move turned sour.

Such comments inevitably lead to speculation over what is really behind the decision if not purely a choice based on driver performance.

As Ferrari-backed Rafa Camara is the favourite to replace Ocon, some sympathetic to Ocon's cause have inferred that Ferrari's support of its junior driver is shoving Ocon out the door.

There have also been some suggestions of Haas prioritising a commercial element. And Ocon has his own detractors too, those who believe he has simply not been good enough after being outscored by team-mate Ollie Bearman over the two years.

Haas had a contractual option to retain Ocon for next year and decided not to activate it quite a long time ago, subsequently notifying Ocon just after the summer break that he was unlikely to be kept on.

It has been a significant shift since Ocon being so highly coveted by Haas. When Ocon was signed, team boss Ayao Komatsu was faced with a lot of questions about whether it would work, though there could be no doubt about Ocon's pedigree coming in.

Not since 10-time podium finisher Romain Grosjean joined for the team's inaugural F1 season in 2016 as Haas employed such a successful driver.

He also arrived carrying the label of sometimes being a difficult driver to work with, who had clashed with team-mates multiple times, and joined after being dropped by Alpine before the final race of 2024 and replaced with Jack Doohan. And was known to disagree with his past teams over the extent of perceived car issues he said were holding him back.

It's also worth remembering that Mercedes ultimately decided Ocon wasn't quite good enough to warrant replacing Valtteri Bottas in the way George Russell ultimately did.

Komatsu was still willing to gamble. It just did not pay off as hoped.

Komatsu, who pushed hard to bring Ocon to the team, felt their previous relationship dating back to Komatsu's time as a senior engineer at what's now Alpine during its Lotus era, when Ocon was a member of the Lotus F1 junior team (pictured together in 2014 below) before Mercedes snapped him up, would help smooth things along and prevent any tensions that arose spilling over.

In one specific aspect this has been a success: Ocon and team-mate Bearman have maintained a good working relationship throughout Ocon's spell with the team, and even when there have been flashpoints, such as a collision at the 2025 British Grand Prix and another at Spa this year, those moments have been addressed internally and fostered no ill-will between the two drivers.

What Komatsu misjudged is how well it would work more broadly. He was fully aware that Ocon had some difficult moments, but put that down to Alpine handling him poorly as that team was going through frequent turmoil and upheaval during its transition from the Cyril Abiteboul regime Ocon began with, to the Flavio Briatore-led one that ousted him.

Haas had to work hard in the early part of 2025 to push past the mental baggage Ocon carried from how he felt he was mistreated during the final races of his Alpine stint, as that team coalesced around Pierre Gasly and edged Ocon toward the exit.

But the team began to notice a worrying pattern: when results didn't go Ocon's way he would become defensive and tensions in the garage would rise and Haas gradually felt there was ultimately a lack of accountability for his own issues.

This is not a problem unique to Ocon. Many drivers get trapped in a paranoid mindset and it's worth remembering the specific background to Ocon's racing career. He got to F1 against all financial odds, with absolutely no silver spoon in his mouth, overcoming adversity right from his earliest days in karting.

So he was probably always more likely than most to have a 'me against the world' mentality. When you have to fight your way into F1 in the first place, that combative streak can be a very powerful weapon - but it can also become all too easily ingrained.

As the defeats to Bearman piled up through the course of 2025, Ocon began repeating complaints publicly about his car, in particular the brakes. At the start of 2026 Haas made a concerted effort to get proper alignment between Ocon and all the staff working on his side of the garage.

But as the year has gone on and Haas has slowly realised it has deeper technical issues itself to deal with, tensions have risen again.

The team ultimately feels Ocon has been too combative internally when backs have been against the wall, as well as questioning car specifications or performance discrepancies, or wasting time on blind-alley set-up work.

This is likely to be a matter of perspective. Ocon almost certainly believes he is just being straightforward, doing the job of trying to push the team forward by being demanding, as was mapped out right from the start - and therefore Haas is simply now using the thing they said they wanted from him originally against him.

Why mini-revival hasn't saved him

Ocon has only occasionally shown the best of himself at Haas. Some excellent race results in his first year were overshadowed by a general qualifying struggle over the season and a particular, inconsistent problem pushing the car on the brakes in the final part of the year.

This year, he missed the small window to score big results when Haas was more competitive before its form declined in the midfield - a mix of his own misjudgement like in China and some genuine misfortune with safety car timings.

That has warped the points situation versus Bearman, who scored 17 of his 20 points in the first two races. Since then it's 7-3 in Ocon's favour. And he has been better than what some seem willing to credit him for.

Haas's decline and the onset of more car inconsistencies - this time on both sides of the garage - have prevented Ocon from doing anything standout to plead his case. This has to be considered a degree of mitigation for Ocon. Bearman said it makes it “really challenging” for the drivers because the behaviour can change completely from track to track. 

Still, even a mini-revival hasn't changed Ocon's fate.

His general performances and attitude did improvesince Haas told him his F1 career with the team was hanging by a thread. And had Ocon performed at the level he's shown since the end of the summer break consistently over the majority of the past 18 months, Haas would view the situation very differently. Ocon would have a strong case for being retained. 

Komatsu rates Ocon very highly when he's at his best, and also likes him as a person - feeling he is a genuinely nice guy when all is well and amicable. It's simply the case that Ocon's working relationship became strained and his time at Haas has been a cycle of short bursts of sustained improvement, followed by a regression to old bad habits.

Taking Baku as an example, where Ocon qualified 13th but beat Bearman to eighth in the race, Haas was left unimpressed by the way Ocon reacted to his Q2 exit in qualifying, failing to take responsibility for an error on his first run then reacting badly to a yellow flag interruption on his second run that Bearman - who also went out in Q2 in the same circumstances - handled much better, despite being the younger and less experienced driver.

Ocon also switched the running order of the cars without informing the team, seen as further evidence Ocon can sometimes act in his own interests rather than those of the team. Although by this time you could argue he knows he's on his way out - so why bother going the extra mile to keep Haas happy?

Ocon's Baku race performance reminds everyone of the calibre of driver Ocon is and what he can bring at his best. But it was not simply a case of too littletoo late, just generally too late.

Money factor is secondary

Other speculation has surrounded Haas's perceived financial uncertainty and claims that owner Gene Haas wants Camara because it will bring in necessary commercial backing.

The eponymous team owner's position is said to be far less involved than that, though. He will just rubber-stamp whatever Komatsu decides or have the final say if there's a close call. There is not an indication that Haas himself is ordering this move or has even guided its direction.

So, where might money have crept into it?

The Race understands that Komatsu told Ocon he was unlikely to be retained in 2027 after the summer break, although it was not a definitive ‘you're out'.

Haas felt that, on the balance of the results and performance levels Ocon had delivered so far, it couldn't justify paying him what is understood to be a multi-million dollar salary.

It's fair to wonder how much of this is purely driven by Ocon failing to justify the money Haas is paying him, and how much is down to the commercial reality of Haas operating below the cost cap and generally being underfunded.

And it's possible that Ocon took this as the team not being willing to pay for a driver of his track record, hence his remarks about there being elements at play behind the scenes that are “out of my control”.

Money was at least a secondary factor in who should replace him. Komatsu has admitted that if two drivers were of equal perceived performance then “affiliations or the packages they've got matters”.

There is an understanding that Camara's arrival will come with commercial benefits from South America that Ocon himself cannot match. That's undeniably to Haas's benefit that Camara comes with a big commercial benefit - from his personal Brazilian backers, rather than Ferrari - but the package he offers is not thought to be at the scale Haas title sponsor Toyota could bring to get current test driver Ryo Hirakawa that seat, for example.

If Haas was purely prioritising money/marketing reasons over competitive considerations, Hirakawa would be the obvious choice here.

But it was agreed he would only get the nod if he was also fastest in the shootout. He wasn't. Toyota knows this and has accepted it.

The prospect of Camara lining up alongside Bearman - long considered a future Ferrari driver and a long-time protege - has caused some to draw unfair comparisons to Red Bull controlling two teams' driver line-ups in F1.

Haas is not a Ferrari-controlled vehicle for it to just test junior drivers. The affiliation affords access and makes it a lot more convenient, so it greases the wheels certainly. But there is no prerequisite and nothing Ferrari can do to force Haas to take a driver it does not want. 

In that sense, Haas likely having an all-Ferrari pairing has been described to The Race as more of a ‘coincidence' than anything else. 

Ocon was never going to be retained over Bearman, considering Bearman's Ferrari support, age, and higher potential, as well as his Max Verstappen-esque tolerance for rear instability in the car.

So, with Bearman set to stay, Ocon had to ward off these external threats to earn his own seat. As these alternatives pressed their case during various Testing Of Previous Cars evaluations, so Haas realised: why pay Ocon for a job they felt, over a season, someone else could do - and potentially do better - without the baggage and hassle following the incumbent driver around?

The emergence of Camara sealed the deal. Haas tested him at Portimao and was blown away by Camara's immense one-lap pace - so strong that, on the day, even Bearman couldn't match him with the reference work he did.

That's not to suggest Camara is quicker than Bearman overall, but it basically serves as evidence that on the shootout day Camara was the standout. Hirakawa came in second best, while McLaren junior Leonardo Fornaroli was fast in steady state conditions but struggled when things became windier and trickier.

Ally that to the professional and focused attitude Camara displayed throughout proceedings, and it was in the end an easy decision for Haas to make - especially once it had decided that Ocon's time at the team needed to come to an end.

items.title: Ocon suddenly replaced at Haas for rest of Mexico F1 weekend
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Esteban Ocon will sit out the rest of Formula 1's Mexican Grand Prix with Haas reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa replacing him.

Haas unexpectedly released a short statement on Saturday morning announcing the switch.

"TGR Haas F1 team reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa will replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix," the statement read.

"Hirakawa, a two-time winner of the FIA World Endurance Championship and 24 Hours of Le Mans Winner with Toyota Gazoo Racing, participated in FP1 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on Friday 30 October - his third free practice outing of the season driving the VF-26, finishing 15th overall.

"The Japanese driver will partner team-mate Ollie Bearman through final practice and qualifying on Saturday and Sunday's 71-lap grand prix - Hirakawa's Formula 1 race debut.

"No further statements will be made at this time."

No reason has been given for the change but Haas has confirmed it is not due to illness for Ocon.

It is logical therefore to reason that he appears to have been benched.

Ocon had a frustrating Friday in Mexico, publicly expressing his dissatisfaction with his runplan in FP2 - his only session in the car, after 32-year-old Hirakawa drove in FP1 to satisfy the rookie practice rule.

His time was not bad - after getting the car back off Hirakawa for FP2, Ocon beat team-mate Ollie Bearman to end up a respectable 13th - but there was friction on the radio with his engineer Laura Mueller.

: We've swapped the high fuel run to medium because Ollie's [tyre] appearance is not great.: Still doing soft, right?: No, we have to do medium.: No, no, I wanted the soft, like, don't do that to me. Come on.

Ocon was visibly dissatisfied in the paddock after the session, keeping his helmet on as he returned to Haas's hospitality unit.

Camara beat the likes of Toyota-backed driver Hirakawa to secure the seat.

Two-time WEC champion Hirakawa has completed multiple F1 practice outings for McLaren, Alpine and Haas since the end of 2024, with a long-stated aim of racing in F1.

The team is making no comment on its driver line-up for the next race in Brazil, in keeping with its statement.

items.title: What F1 teams have done to tackle Mexico's altitude challenge
items.author: Gary Anderson
items.content:
The Mexico City track is one of the outliers of the Formula 1 season, mainly because of the altitude: it is 2240 meters above sea level, which equates to roughly 25% less dense air, so it makes everything just that bit more difficult.

For the drivers it's basically harder work, but for the cars it's a very different story, because at that altitude the cars will produce less downforce and with that less drag. In the past, teams would use more or less Monaco-specification wings but this season with the change in wing regulations and active aero they don't have that possibility.

So, basically the ars will slide around more but the reduced drag means that top speeds are even faster than normal. This means that you will arrive at the end of those long straights faster and require a longer braking duration, which generates more heat in the brakes.

These cars are turbocharged so in reality even though the turbo has to work harder and will be running at or as near to its maximum rpm as possible for most of the lap, it will still produce similar levels of power output. This means the engine's heat rejection isn't reduced, so you need to cool the cars roughly 25% more than you normally have to.

Also, as it's an electrical energy-rich circuit layout you will also generate more heat into the battery pack and its control systems simply from harvesting and deployment.

Basically, everything needs higher levels of cooling and below I have had a look at the top-four teams' changes from what they normally run. It's not easy to alter the inlet area on these cars as it is part of the side impact structure, so changing it would basically require redoing the side impact tests, so instead everyone will focus on the cooling exits, size, location and quantity.

First of all we can have a look at the rear exits.

The red ellipse highlights the rearwards-facing outlet. McLaren has raised the section above the exhaust outlet to increase the exit area.

It already ran a spec-two outlet at Austin and as can be seen by the red ellipse Mercedes has retained that for Mexico. Now it is more of a triangular opening, which it has achieved by lifting the upper engine cover surface, especially in the central section, above the exhaust outlet.

Ferrari has gone for simply a bigger exit at the sides, as highlighted by the two green ellipses. The central section is similar in height to the previous version.

From what I can see, Red Bull hasn't really bothered to alter the outlet in this area.

The rear exits are in more or less the same position and, in reality, are more or less the same size for all the teams - so the effect they have on the overall cars efficiency will be well understood.

When you are getting the maximum from that area then it's onto the sidepod and engine-cover louvre outlets. This is the most critical area as far as maximising the cooling is concerned, and major changes in this area can affect the airflow structure of the rest of the car coming along behind. It's not just about bigger louvres, it's more about placement relative to the body-surface pressure and how and where those louvres are placed can have a major influence.

The top two cars in this comparison, Mercedes and Ferrari, are fairly similar in placement and both have two fairly well-defined locations. These positions are normally placed where the internal radiator flow is at its weakest.

The McLaren on the other hand has a more aesthetically pleasing placing and the fact that it all connects together also adds to the aesthetics. My sentiments are that as long as it achieves the objective, why go for ugly when it can be visually appealing to the eye?

Red Bull on the other hand externally looks like it has made the fewest changes to compensate for the altitude in Mexico. Perhaps it was overcooled at other races but I would doubt this - as most teams will push the limits for each individual track.

That's all the engine and its ancillary cooling requirement changes compared. The other big cooling requirement is for the brakes and it's difficult to see who has done the best job there.

For the teams, it's difficult to simulate those early race laps when the car is at its heaviest and you are running in traffic; when the brakes overheat, the only way to cool them down is to use them less - which means more lifting and coasting.

So, who has done the best job on all of this while minimising the aerodynamic losses? I think it's going to be Sunday night before we know that.

items.title: Why F1's 2026 cars are unusually quick in Mexico
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
A combination of factors means Formula 1's 2026 cars have been unusually close to the performance of their ground-effect predecessors in Mexico.

Charles Leclerc's FP1-topping time, a 1m18.128s, was 0.252s quicker than the lap he set to lead first practice in Mexico last year. That's the first time the 2026 cars have outpaced the 2025 cars in an FP1 session, having usually been two or three seconds slower.

Leclerc lowered the bar by three tenths to a 1m17.827s in FP2, though that was 0.435s slower than Max Verstappen's FP2 benchmark from last year.

Pirelli's pre-weekend simulations had predicted a 1m17.0s would be pole position, but after Friday's running it's now predicted to be well below that.

Pole position last year - a 1m15.586s - ended up being 1.8s faster than the pace in FP2, so you'd expect the 2026 pole position to be in the low-1m16s.

That should mean the smallest 2025 versus 2026 dry-weather qualifying difference of the season, with the previous closest being 1.409s in Baku.

So why are the 2026 cars so competitive at the Mexican Grand Prix relative to their ground-effect-era predecessors?

A resurfaced, busier track

The track underwent a partial resurfacing ahead of the 2026 race, with resurfacing work taking place from Turn 10 to Turn 1.

"This could also be an effect," Pirelli's chief engineer Simone Berra said.

"Obviously it was partially resurfaced, so sector one and half of sector two didn't have this kind of new Tarmac, so that could be a contribution also, but it's not the only explanation about why we were so fast, or faster than we expected."

Another explanation Pirelli offered is the track being in better condition because there's more support series laying down rubber this year.

However, there has only been a 10-minute increase in the on-track action prior to FP1 versus last year, with the one-make GTM Super Copa series, Masters Historic and Formula 4 NACAM championship on the support bill this year.

"I think part of these results are due to the track in better conditions compared to last year, we have several supporting series that are helping," Berra said.

"All the supporting series run before FP1 and between FP1 and FP2, so the track was evolving quite a lot during the day."

Less of a penalty at altitude

The most important factor is Mexico's high altitude is also less detrimental to the performance of the 2026 cars and power units than the 2025 packages. There's less total downforce to lose in the first place and the ground-effect cars were more downforce-dependent.

"The conditions, the altitude here, it's in favour of these cars compared to the old one," Berra said.

"The old cars were losing more downforce, compared to what this car generation are losing.

"Also, the other point is that the engine can push more compared to a normal situation or sea level conditions.

"So that's the main point, the drivers can push and so the difference with laptimes from last year are reduced."

Altitude, of course, does not effect the electrical power, which is far more influential on performance with the 2026 power units.

The 2026 cars (Leclerc's lap in red) are quicker on the straights than the 2025 cars (Verstappen's lap in blue), with the 2026 machines over four tenths up on the run to the Turn 4 left-hander. And it should be noted that Leclerc's Ferrari is one of the weakest in this section among the top-four teams because of its power unit deficit. So the gap is even larger if you compare to Verstappen's 2026 car.

The 2026 cars quickly lose that built-up advantage in the low-speed corners that follow and never recover it, but the drop-off is far less stark than at other circuits such as Spa (3.799s between 2025 and 2026 poles) and Monza (2.994s between them).

The cars actually end up relatively energy-rich in Mexico, so it's one of the better tracks for showcasing the performance of these cars.

items.title: Winners and losers from MotoGP's Sepang sprint
items.author: Eden Hannigan
items.content:
Sepang produced another chaotic MotoGP sprint, as Pedro Acosta walked away with the race victory and Marc Marquez established an ever-increasing grip on the riders’ title. 

After the 10-lap sprint in near-mixed conditions, here are our winners and losers.

Winner: Pedro Acosta (1st)

Out of Acosta's three various-distance race wins in MotoGP so far, this one may well be the nicest - though he admitted it owed a lot to him having no championship implications to worry about unlike Marquez and Marco Bezzecchi.

Considering he isn't really convinced about his strengths in this kind of mixed weather, this was an important win, too, and certainly not something that would dissuade you if you have him pegged as a 2027 title favourite.

Winner: Marc Marquez (2nd)

Marquez marches on, muffling the heartbeats of the already on-life-support title battle. 

This was a slightly precarious race, though not quite as precarious as it could've been. It was just controllable enough for Marquez to control it exactly to his liking - as his gameplan was to stay ahead of Bezzecchi but also to not lead, to not be the pathfinder having to figure out the wet patches.

It worked out well, and while he should have been beaten by his brother today, he wasn't, meaning that it's now been 12 races (across GPs and sprints) since Marquez last wasn't the top Ducati in the classification.

Loser: Alex Marquez (DNF)

It’s not too far-fetched to say the younger Marquez was a pre-weekend contender for a potential 37-point haul, and he looked well on-course when he took pole position and built up a healthy lead three laps into the sprint.

His error that might’ve come from “too much confidence” after his first pole since the 2025 Catalan GP or being “too optimistic” going into Turn 14 threw away a very likely 12 points - and, already injured, it's fortunate he's come away unscathed from what was a fairly high-speed off.

“It’s something tomorrow that we need to control a bit more,” was Marquez’s assessment of that specific corner. At least he’s lucky to have a second go at it, and he normally learns his lessons from Saturday to Sunday. 

Loser: Jack Miller (DNF) and Pramac Yamaha

Everybody involved is more than a little lucky here that the rain didn't unfold like Miller thought it might in pitting at the end of the second lap.

Running 18th, with no hope of points, and aware that a deluge was coming at some point, Miller hoped to pre-empt it by pitting - and arrived to a spare bike that hadn't been swapped to wets.

"I had a chat with Giacomo [Guidotti, crew chief] before the race, I said 'have the bike ready'," Miller explained afterwards. 

"In my mind that was, like, have the bike ready immediately. In his mind that was, like, four-five laps. So, miscommunication and unfortunately today we look like w***ers."

Luckily for Pramac, Miller's gamble would have never worked with the way the rain played out. But imagine if a potential win had been thrown away in this way.

So close to a maiden sprint victory but coming up short due to his lack of wet-weather confidence, it was still an impressive display of (mostly) contained aggression from Ogura. 

Getting a good launch from the second row of the grid, Ogura went all-out against Marquez in the opening corners of the sprint, and eventually got the better of the Ducati rider throughout the first phase of the race.

It didn’t last, thanks to the mixed conditions the Trackhouse Aprilia rider hates, and he crossed the line in fourth, which was still a mega effort and also much better than Ogura himself had anticipated.

“Last in the group, so there’s no reason to be happy,” was his ever self-critical description.

Winner: Brad Binder (7th)

Yes, Binder's seventh place pales in comparison with what Acosta managed eight seconds up the road - but you take the wins where you can get them, and Binder badly needed one this weekend.

He has looked totally out of sorts over one lap here, worse than usual, but basically undid all the damage from a poor qualifying into Turn 1.

There was a bit of back-and-forth combat from there, and some wet-weather improvisation, so it's not a huge surprise Binder came off well - beating Enea Bastianini and only just coming up short of picking off Pecco Bagnaia.

Winner: Diogo Moreira (8th)

Moreira made his life a bit harder than it needed to be with a mistake early on in the race - but was afforded the opportunity to make up for it by the weather.

He seemed to thrive in the cagey late-race conditions relative to those around him, working his way past the battling duo of Johann Zarco and Enea Bastianini for a rock-solid eighth place.

In the context of just this race, the performance of the two remaining Aprilias was actually pretty good considering Sepang has long been one of its nemesis circuits for the RS-GP. 

However, in the broader scheme of 2026, where it just lost its most valuable asset in Jorge Martin and is praying for a miracle with Bezzecchi, it’s a circuit where it cannot afford to be outscored by Marquez. 

But that’s exactly what happened on Saturday, despite the best efforts of Ogura to disrupt the Ducati rider’s momentum. In a race that threatened chaos, it could have been one to upset Marquez, and it just didn't.

Similarly, Bezzecchi could have thrown caution to the wind and just gone for it, knowing he has no pressure and no real championship chance. He didn’t, only passing Ogura - who steadfastly denied Aprilia orders hinted at by Marquez.

Ogura's denial rings true, but nobody would really begrudge Aprilia if it did want to try to keep its riders' title aspirations alive through team orders. As it stands, even team orders would be nowhere near enough.

items.title: How Herta compared to Perez in latest 2027 audition
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Colton Herta might still somehow be one point short of a Formula 1 superlicence after a bizarre error, but his latest Cadillac F1 outing was an important audition to replace Valtteri Bottas next year.

An incorrect calculation of his superlicence points (verified at the time by the FIA) means Herta erroneously thought completing 30 laps in his fifth FP1 outing of the season in Mexico would be enough to take him to the 40-point threshold required to finally earn him the superlicence he's been chasing for years.

"I was literally walking to go do the media stuff [after FP2], that was like the first time I had heard about it," Herta said on Friday evening. 

"Obviously, we were still doing our meetings and whatnot, so I haven't talked to anybody about it. As far as I was concerned, going into the weekend, if I did 100km here, I would have 40 [points]. 

"So, I'm not sure what's changed, or why stuff has changed, or if it even has. I have to wait and see. I think a lot of the people that I want to talk to about this are still in the meeting. Maybe I'll have a little bit more clarity this evening." 

Cadillac has gone beyond the mandated four rookie practice outings and given Herta a fifth session in Mexico to get him an extra point. It will run him again to get the final point, and had planned to anyway before the bizarre calculation error emerged. 

But his Mexico outing wasn't a case of Herta simply cruising around to get the mandated 100km of running to get the point. He was given an extensive programme that wasn't too dissimilar to the one conducted by Perez - his 2027 team-mate, should Herta secure Bottas's race seat. 

Herta's FP1 starts with an 11-lap stint on the hard tyres with a best lap of 1m22.452s, 1.067s slower than Perez's on the same tyres.

Herta tells his engineer he's "leaving a lot on the table" in sector one, but he's told that's where he's actually faster than Perez; instead, he's leaking time in sectors two and three. 

This continues when he switches to the medium tyres, completing back-to-back stints on them with only a brief pitstop to go half a turn down on the front wing - a microadjustment to reduce the angle.

It's on that second run when Herta completes his personal best lap, a 1m21.365s, on what are seven-lap-old tyres. 

Perez, by contrast, is able to complete his fastest lap on three-lap-old tyres during his first medium-tyre stint.

The actual gap between them is 0.970s. Perez puts together his best three sectors; if you combine Herta's, he closes slightly to 0.817s. 

The Esses, in particular the Turn 10/11 right-left, are particularly challenging for Herta as he has to abandon one lap on the hard tyres when he cuts that corner, while another is wrecked by a wide moment there. 

He complained of "big understeer everywhere in the low-speed" corners. He struggled with his approach into the Turn 12 right-hander that leads into the stadium section; Herta's minimum speed drops to 13km/h below Perez's, so here alone he ships around four tenths to Perez on their fastest short runs. 

"The biggest thing was figuring out the timing for Turn 12," Herta said when The Race asked what his biggest limitation was.

"The stadium section I think was all right. More so Turn 12. And then kind of sorted it out for the long run.

"It's hard for the performance runs. You only do so many laps to sort it out in time. So unfortunately I didn't do that well. But for the long run it was better."

Herta's claim stacks up as he generally halves that time loss in Turn 12 during his longer run at the end of the session.

This is on average around eight tenths slower than Perez's, although it's hard to know the exact fuel loads of both cars.

Herta called it the "most consistent part of my running", and the data backs that up with only a half-second variation in his laptimes over a seven-lap stint. A decent effort for a driver inexperienced in F1 machinery.

Watching his FP1 onboard versus Perez, it was clear Herta needed more steering input around the lap and he was advised to better manage his throttle usage out of Turn 11 - corner exits being key to getting the most out of the 2026 power units.

He's still adapting from his usual aggressive style that worked so well for him in IndyCar, "where without power steering you can be more aggressive".

"You can have two or three or four inputs into the corner [in IndyCar], whereas in the Formula 1 car it's kind of useless effort," said Herta.

"You have to be smooth and really precise with the line. Whereas in IndyCar you can maybe get away with a little bit more of a raggedy style.

"Really, that's just down to the lack of power steering in the IndyCar."

F1 superlicence will be 'monkey off my back'

Asked if he saw himself as a realistic contender for the 2027 Cadillac seat, Herta said: "I hope so. I don't know why I'd be doing this [otherwise].

"I think Cadillac has shown a lot of faith in me in doing all these FP1s. They put a lot of resources behind me to get me ready to be in the F1 seat.

"I hope that's all reciprocated, and I can make it."

He added: "As far as 'now or never' - I don't think I can go back to IndyCar and have another chance in Formula 1. Whether that means next year or the following year. I really don't know what the plan is at the moment.

"We'll have to wait and see. I think some decisions hopefully will be made within the next month.

"It would be great the sooner the better to know going into November. You want to know what you're doing next year. For me, that's the main thing, is to know what I'm doing next year."

Herta said "social media blows things up a lot more than in reality" so he's remaining calm amid rumours of him graduating to F1.

But he did admit it will be a relief when he finally gets to the 40 superlicence points.

"Just maximising. Doing everything better. There's always time to find," Herta said when asked what he wants from his next FP1 outing.

"Just being able to maximise the short run and being able to maximise the long run. Probably a bit more in the short run than the long run.

"But I think every time I get in the car I feel more comfortable and I'm able to push a bit more.

"So I think once I kind of get that superlicence and that monkey off my back, then you can really kind of push everything as hard as you want to."

The Race understands Cadillac was impressed with the job Herta did in Mexico, even if his ultimate pace was adrift of Perez's.

It sees solid progression along Herta's F1 outings, and he remains a strong contender for a 2027 seat. At the same time, so do incumbent Bottas and the likes of Yuki Tsunoda and Mercedes reserve driver Fred Vesti.

Vesti was particularly brash after FP1, where he was only 0.111s adrift of championship leader Kimi Antonelli in the sister Mercedes.

"I've got my eyes on that [Cadillac] seat," he said. "I believe I would be very, very good in that car, and to be in F1 has been my goal ever since I started driving.

"I'm more motivated than ever; I'm extremely hungry to be on the grid."

George Russell, who Vesti replaced for FP1, even said he told Mercedes: "I want to ensure that he [Vesti] gets an opportunity to show what he can do; that's the least that we could do."

It was probably as strong an audition as Vesti could have hoped to make for the seat.

And he wasn't the only rookie to set an eye-catching pace in FP1.

Tsolov's impressive debut

Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov made the most of his F1 weekend debut to make his case for promotion to a race seat next year, lapping just 0.13s off Arvid Lindblad based on their headline laptimes on softs, and lapping two tenths quicker on mediums.

To that we must add the caveat that there was evidence of differing energy strategies, with Lindblad often faster on the back straight and Tsolov stronger on the main straight - with Lindblad suffering one of the most extreme drop-offs in speed in the field prior to braking for Turn 1.

Although Tsolov had a couple of laps deleted for track-limits violations, he was a little quicker than Lindblad in sector three, although he consistently lost time through and out of Turn 3. He was also perhaps a little conservative on the brakes into Turn 1 at the start of his best lap, perhaps not helped by the distraction of Isack Hadjar's Red Bull cruising off line approaching the corner. This was on the third push lap of his performance run on softs.

Tsolov also had a problem with the seat impeding the bloodflow to his right leg. After setting his fastest lap, he reported that "I'm running out of blood in my right leg, I cannot feel my leg", and then suggested that "the seat is compressing my leg and my blood stopped". He returned to the garage and was able to return to the cockpit for another run after briefly standing up inside the car.

"I've actually had that a few times before driving in F2," said Tsolov. "It's just the seat, I think, being a bit tighter than what we would like in my right leg. So my blood closed off.

"When you press the full throttle, you move up into the seats, so you kind of compress your legs. That was the thing, I couldn't feel it. It was a dead leg, pretty much. You get the tingly feeling. And then it just came back, obviously. I had to shake it out and after two, three minutes, it came back."

Slater's 'difficult' F1 debut

Formula 3 runner-up Freddie Slater's F1 session debut was best summed up by the radio message he received, in which it was described as "a very difficult session from a technical point of view".

That was an understatement, as he took the chequered flag after completing only 13 laps spread across six runs. Not that this was through any fault of the 18-year-old's.

He started out with three single-lap runs. The first two of those focused on gathering aerodynamic data, with aero rakes mounted behind the front wheel and a nose change in between.

He then should have been able to settle into a longer run on the hard Pirellis starting on his fifth lap, only to be told "we have to box this lap, we have an issue", entering Turn 7. This was because a fan had been left in the right-side sidepod cooling inlet, meaning Audi was fined €7500 for releasing the car in an unsafe condition.

The team then sent Slater back out, but he was immediately called back in for a lengthy stay in the garage.

He was able to return to the track with 11 minutes remaining, on a set of mediums. On his first push lap of the session, he posted a 1m22.451s, running deep in Turn 6 and compromising Turn 7. Then, on the second attempt, he locked up the front-left into Turn 1 and had to cut across the grass.

The resulting flatspot meant he had to pit to switch back to hards, on which he had one push lap that stood at his fastest of the session - elevating him to 21st ahead of Herta. That put him 1.337s behind team-mate Nico Hulkenberg, which in the circumstances of his disrupted session and posting his best time on hards on only his second full flying lap was very respectable.

"It's motorsport and that's how things go," said Slater of his stop-start running.

"Of course, it was a bit frustrating obviously not to get many, many laps, but overall that one lap that I did do was actually pretty good compared to relevant data. And a really historic day for Audi to have their first junior driver in the car.

"It's a very special day, so we look at the positives and then we focus on the results."

items.title: Acosta wins chaotic Sepang MotoGP sprint
items.author: Eden Hannigan
items.content:
Pedro Acosta claimed victory in a bizarre Sepang MotoGP sprint that was threatened by rain late on.

Acosta came out on top of a four-way battle for the race win, prevailing by 0.578s over Marc Marquez, who increased his championship chances with second place.

Marquez is now 19 points up on the absent Jorge Martin, and 52 points clear of Marco Bezzecchi.

His brother Alex Marquez had got the start from pole position and led uncontested for four laps until he slid out of the race lead at Turn 14.

The lead was then inherited by Ai Ogura, who had moved up to second place after an aggressive opening corner tussle with Marc.

Spots of rain meant the white flag came out on lap two, allowing riders to swap bikes - with Jack Miller immediately prepared to take the gamble, but his Pramac Yamaha team not ready with his second bike, which frustrated him to no end.

Iker Lecuona, Joan Mir and Franco Morbidelli were the first group to come in and successfully switch on lap five, but were setting times almost 10 seconds off the leaders’ pace, with Maverick Vinales the only other rider electing to change towards the end of the race.

In the tricky conditions the top four bunched up, Ogura managing to hold off the challenges until Acosta attacked with three laps to spare.

Although Ogura responded to the initial overtake from Acosta, he eventually ceded the position and slumped to fourth as his wet-weather demons made him no match for Marquez and Bezzecchi. He did, however, have a huge amount of breathing room to fifth-placed Fabio Di Giannantonio.

Pecco Bagnaia overcame Brad Binder in their battle for sixth, while Diogo Moreira and Enea Bastianini picked up the final sprint points in eighth and ninth.

items.title: Martin admits MotoGP title 'already lost' after Sepang withdrawal
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Aprilia MotoGP rider Jorge Martin feels the 2026 title is "already lost" following his withdrawal from the Malaysian Grand Prix weekend - but intends to ride in Qatar next week.

Martin sustained a distal radius fracture in a crash during the Phillip Island sprint, but was back to riding just six days later at Sepang, in a desperate bid to keep himself in the championship picture and minimise the damage versus points leader Marc Marquez.

But Martin was forced to give up on his weekend after three sessions, withdrawing after Saturday morning practice.

"I tried, I tried my best, I tried to ride, but for sure the process of healing is still early," he explained afterwards.

"The healing is going really fast, but not enough to be efficient on the bike. I felt that I could ride with almost no pain, but for maybe one lap. After that I started to have a lot of pain, I couldn't be constant, so watching a bit the laptimes and my performance, we decided to stop, to try to wait.

"We thought together with the team that the effort I was doing was too much to continue and yeah, nothing to gain. It was just going to be very difficult even to score one point."

Martin said he just didn't have the requisite strength under braking - and made reference to his past efforts to shortcut recovery periods, particularly in an injury-laden 2025 and specifically in his return to racing in Qatar last year, in which he ran out of energy in the race, crashed and suffered a bad injury after being hit by a rival bike.

"It wasn't the best idea to continue," he said of this weekend, "because if I continue, it [shows] that I haven't learned anything from the past.

"This happened to me in the past and I didn't want to crash or have a worse injury because of trying to race like this."

Asked by The Race how he views the championship picture in light of his withdrawal, Martin admitted: "I think now I don't have to think about the championship. Maybe I can win it, but for me it's already lost.

"So for sure I will fight till the end, not only for me, because at the end of the day I'm already a champion [in 2024], but for my team, for my people, I will fight till the end, I will try again in Qatar. Otherwise I would stay at home and rest."

Martin trails Marquez by 10 points, with Marquez in position to triple or quadruple that lead at Sepang, having placed second in qualifying.

Though Martin will return to Spain right away, as referenced above he still intends to try and race in Qatar next weekend, assuming that round goes ahead.

"During this week the improvement was incredible. I was able to ride a MotoGP with a broken wrist, so it's crazy. And I was under two minutes [in laptime]! So I'm already proud of my performance.

"My target is to go to Qatar. I will go there and I will try. Then if my feeling is the same, then I will have to stop. But this we will see in Qatar."

items.title: Martin out of Sepang MotoGP weekend, Alex Marquez on pole
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Alex Marquez took pole position for MotoGP's Malaysian Grand Prix and the sprint, as title hopeful Jorge Martin withdrew from the Sepang weekend.

Martin, who fractured his wrist a week ago at Phillip Island, did three runs totalling eight laps in the 30-minute practice session before qualifying, and had to concede defeat in terms of continuing with the weekend.

"His feeling was better, to be honest, compared with yesterday, but he was not able to force in the braking," Aprilia team manager Paolo Bonora told MotoGP.com.

"The plan is to come back to Spain as soon as possible and to push on the recovery and to do his best to recover the situation. Coming back to Spain immediately, and then we check all together, during all the days, the situation, how it is improving, and we focus to have him in Qatar."

With Martin now consigned to a non-score at Sepang, points leader Marc Marquez was close to maximising his qualifying, ultimately just 0.070s short of beating his brother.

Alex Marquez had been the leader after the initial Q2 runs already, but was shuffled down to fifth by the end of the session - only to respond with a 1m56.493s that snatched pole from Marc.

Pedro Acosta on the KTM will join the pair on the front row, having followed the elder Marquez very closely on both Q2 runs.

Aprilia pair Ai Ogura and Marco Bezzecchi completed a top five covered by just 0.175s, with Fabio Di Giannantonio in sixth another 0.174s back from Bezzecchi.

Q1 pace-setter Johann Zarco was limited to just one Q2 run but used Di Giannantonio as reference and so helped himself to eighth place, slotting in on row three between Enea Bastianini and Franco Morbidelli.

Pecco Bagnaia, another Q1 graduate, ran 'off-sequence' in Q2 - doing his sole run mid-session, with no riders around him.

After setting what proved to be his fastest lap he went off at Turn 1 and broke the windscreen in anger with his fist - though would have anyway been unlikely to improve.

He placed 10th, ahead of Joan Mir and the injury-limited Maverick Vinales, who could not match his laptime from Friday.

Honda riders Luca Marini and Diogo Moreira trailed stablemate Zarco by three and four tenths respectively in Q1, so were short of advancing into Q2 - while the rest of the field was never really in the mix.

This included Gresini's Fermin Aldeguer stand-in Iker Lecuona, who has found Sepang the most difficult so far of the tracks he's ridden this season as a MotoGP replacement rider.

items.title: Ferrari is fastest in Mexico - but not for reasons rivals expected
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Ferrari’s rivals were right after all, but perhaps for the wrong reasons.

The talk ahead of the Mexico Grand Prix had been that Ferrari’s smaller turbo design would give it a clear advantage at the high altitude track because it would in theory struggle less in the thinner air.

So there was little surprise in the paddock when Charles Leclerc delivered a clean sweep of fastest laps in both FP1 and FP2 on Friday - confirming the Prancing Horse as the team to beat.

What was perhaps more interesting from what we saw though - and which could play a big role in how the rest of the weekend plays out - was that Ferrari’s advantage was not coming from its turbo getting its boost pressure up quicker.

Ferrari’s straight-line speed performance was notably lacking on the second and third straights. On its soft runs Leclerc was slowest of the top four teams into Turns 4 and 12.

As Lewis Hamilton, who was sidelined by a suspected power unit problem halfway through FP2, remarked: “If you look at the speeds to the Mercedes and the Red Bull, they're still massive.

"They're still quicker at the end of the straights, like they are in every race. So the turbo is just not making a difference. They are still pulling more at the end of the straights.

“I think we're still losing a good two or three tenths. But the car is behaving really well fundamentally. Our car works really well, seemingly on a track like this.”

Ferrari’s advantage in Mexico instead was coming from an area it has excelled in all season - low speed corner performance.

It was just marginally better through the first two complexes of corners (Turns 1-3 plus Turns 4-6) as well as taking a decent chunk out of the opposition from Turn 12 into the stadium section.

That trait meant that Leclerc had the consistency needed from the tyres to deliver the strongest long run of the afternoon - leaving rivals in no doubt about who was the benchmark.

But while the opposition clearly was happy to put that favourite status on Ferrari, that does not necessarily mean that all hope is lost for everyone else.

Others certainly saw enough in the data to think that there remains a big opportunity to fight at the front.

When we look at the long run averages, Lando Norris in the McLaren, plus the Mercedes and Red Bulls were not far behind what Leclerc delivered once you factor in the influence of cool down laps and traffic.

Mexican GP FP2 long run averagesRussell (soft): 1m21.442s

Antonelli (medium): 1m21.487s

Leclerc (medium): 1m21.163s

Piastri (soft): 1m21.642s

Norris (soft): 1m21.319s

Verstappen (soft): 1m21.490s

Hadjar (soft): 1m21.369s

It was a day where certainly not everybody delivered to their maximum, as drivers battled brake locking, bumps and rapidly rising tyre temperatures.

George Russell said: “Ferrari looked very strong and that was kind of the anticipation ahead of the weekend

“I think we are still not fully on top of the new package, I think we see there's some balance limitations we have that we're struggling to overcome.

"I would say currently for Kimi and I, we're probably more outside the window, similar to what we saw in Malaysia, than inside the window like Kimi [Antonelli] achieved in Austin. Hopefully overnight we can get it back there."

Things perhaps being a bit closer than they look at first glance is even more in play when you take into account that Verstappen’s afternoon was derailed by his clash with Liam Lawson that damaged his floor.

That left the Dutchman battling a disconnected balance throughout his long run as he was lacking some key parts - so you could anticipate a potential improvement there.

As Red Bull’s technical director Pierre Wache said: “Let's see tomorrow when the floor will be repaired and how the car is better or not.”

Wache certainly felt that Ferrari was not out of reach, especially considering it has been strong in the types of turns that Mexico is full of.

“I think in low-speed corners, since the beginning of the year, they are clearly on top of the game, and they have clearly a lot of downforce for low speed. After, let's see what we can extract. I think we are not far, and hope we can challenge them.”

While the indications are of an early Ferrari advantage based on what we have seen so far, there are some important factors that mean it still cannot sleep easy tonight.

The first element is that the long runs on Friday may not be totally representative of how things will play out in the race because of track temperature variations.

The late start for FP2, allied to conditions being a bit cooler, meant that the track surface was not as hot as it will be on Sunday.

Wache said it was not nailed on which would be the optimum tyre for the race.

“The tyres are overheating in the last sector,” he said. “Clearly, the main problem is in FP2 where the track [temp] reduced by more than 10 degrees.

“For the long run it was not very representative of what we'll see in the race Sunday. Then we have to be very careful on that aspect. So the deg will be higher, and maybe the medium will be better.”

The premium on cooling around Mexico means that the pace of the cars is limited more by managing that than their theoretical best - so that could have a big impact too on how things play out on Sunday.

Overtaking is already difficult here and following close behind a rival becomes far from ideal because of the consequences of engine and brake temperatures - so it is rarely a race where cars come through the field for the win. Clean air is invaluable.

The need for Ferrari to not be in the pack is further increased by its expected turbo advantage having not manifested itself with superb top speed - something rivals were happy to see.

As McLaren’s Oscar Piastri said: “I don’t think the turbo’s going to make as much of a difference as we thought.

“They if anything looked a bit slow on the straights so, let’s wait and see tomorrow, definitely in some circumstances it will help them but I think in normal conditions it’s not as big of a factor as we first feared.”

Put the 'track position is king' element on top of a likely one-stopper where there will not be strategy variation and it puts a huge premium on single-lap pace and delivering what is needed in Q3 to take pole position.

And how many Fridays this season have ended with Ferrari topping the timesheets, looking to have the long-run potential, but then falling flat when things get serious on Saturday afternoon? We only need to go back one weekend for the last time that happened.

Ferrari knows it has a weakness on Saturday based on it not being able to get its tyres as perfectly into the operating window as its rivals - and that could well prove critical in that fight at Mexico.

As Hamilton remarked after practice: “I think the car feels like it's capable of competing in qualifying. But I don't know what it is they [the others] do in quali. Everyone seems to take a step. I don’t know if we can eke out a little bit more tomorrow.”

At a track where the lack of downforce means tyres are sliding a lot more, everything may well come down to looking after those rears.

Even Norris, who was second quickest in the afternoon, reckoned that the key would be delivering at the right moment.

“The pace is definitely there but the field is incredibly tight at the minute, so it will come down to execution in tomorrow’s qualifying,” he said.

Ferrari team boss Fred Vasseur knows that rivals have maybe not got things together as well as hoped on Friday and will come back stronger.

So with things looking as tight as they are, amid what he says are “mega extreme” conditions, the fight for pole - which could be critical to the win - may well come down to simply who can keep their tyres alive the longest in qualifying.

“It's always a challenge in Mexico,” said Vasseur. “I think it was last year that everybody was in half a tenth until Turn 10 and then you had four-tenths’ difference in two corners. I think it will be the same tomorrow.”

items.title: Hadjar summoned for alleged paddock misconduct
items.author: Samarth Kanal
items.content:
Isack Hadjar has been summoned by the stewards after alleged misconduct in the Formula 1 paddock at the Mexican Grand Prix.

The FIA stewards called the Red Bull driver to see them for "misconduct relating to an incident in the Formula 1 paddock".

The summons does not specify why Hadjar has been summoned.

A video has circulated on social media appearing to show Hadjar pushing someone who tried to take a selfie with him. It is however unclear whether this is the reason Hadjar has been called to see the stewards at 10.15am local time on Saturday.

As per the FIA's International Sporting Code, "any words, deeds or writings that have caused moral injury or loss to the FIA, its bodies, its members or its executive officers, and more generally on the interest of motorsport and on the values defended by the FIA" can carry a fine of up to €5000.

Fines of up to €20,000 can be applied in other cases and the FIA's sporting code says: "For very serious offences, more severe penalties under the ISC [international sporting code] may be imposed."

Aggravating or mitigating circumstances can however change the penalty imposed.

items.title: Verstappen and Lawson get grid drops for 'clumsy' Mexico clash
items.author: Jack Cozens
items.content:
Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson have each been given one-place grid penalties for their "clumsy" clash during second Formula 1 practice at the Mexican Grand Prix.

That incident occurred early in FP2 when Verstappen, on a prep lap, tried to lunge past Lawson - on a cooldown lap before another push - into the 90-degree Turn 12 right-hander.

Lawson stayed on the outside of Verstappen through that corner, which became the inside line for the Turn 13 switchback in the stadium section, before Verstappen cut across the track at Turn 14 and got ahead of the Racing Bulls driver, though only via contact that shattered the Red Bull's left-side bargeboard, with the resulting debris prompting a red flag.

Verstappen told Sky Sports F1 it was "not very smart behaviour" from Lawson, who (alongside team-mate Arvid Lindblad) has not yet been announced at Racing Bulls for 2027 and whom Verstappen characterised as "fighting for your seat".

Verstappen said of the incident: "At the end of the day, it's not going to change my weekend."

But the clash did have consequences.

In identical statements issued to both cars, the stewards said they considered both drivers' actions "unacceptable", in particular in respect of a "warning" given at the team managers' meeting earlier on Friday.

They said both Lawson and Verstappen had called the move "clumsy" and unnecessary - a word also used by Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane when describing the contact.

It was that message given at the team managers' meeting that ultimately condemned Verstappen and Lawson to penalties.

"Noting that there had been similar incidents this year of actions between drivers in free practice, the stewards have decided to escalate the penalty from that of a formal warning to a grid position penalty particularly in view of the warning that had been provided at the team managers' meeting and consistent with other incidents involving contact between the cars in free practice in previous years," the stewards' decision read.

Both drivers were also given one penalty point for the transgression.
